desc:
Vertical walls stand along a line: wall i is at position i and has height heights[i]. You want to place a square tank (axis-aligned, standing on the ground) between two walls i < j. It must fit horizontally in the gap, so its side is at most j - i, and it must not rise above the lower of the two walls, so its side is at most min(heights[i], heights[j]).

Return the largest possible area of such a square, over all choices of two walls.

heights = [3, 9, 2, 2, 8, 3, 1]
walls 1 and 4: gap 3, heights 9 and 8  ->  side 3, area 9
result = 9
hints: Checking every pair of walls is O(n²). Think of the classic container problem: start with the widest pair and shrink.
The side is min(h[i], h[j], j - i). Look at the lower wall of the current pair: how large can any pair that keeps this wall but is narrower become?
Keep l = 0, r = n - 1. Record min(h[l], h[r], r - l), then move the pointer at the lower wall inward. (If the walls are equal either one can move.)
editorial: Start with the widest pair and compute its side s = min(h[l], h[r], r - l). Suppose h[l] ≤ h[r]. Any other pair that still uses wall l has a partner j < r, so its width is smaller and its side is bounded by min(h[l], width) ≤ min(h[l], r - l). Since h[l] ≤ h[r], that bound equals the side we just recorded. So no pair using wall l with a closer partner can beat the current pair, and wall l can be discarded (l += 1).

The same argument works symmetrically when h[r] is the lower wall. Every step discards one wall, so after n - 1 steps all candidates have been covered and the answer is the square of the best side seen. This is O(n) time and O(1) space; the brute force is O(n²).
The extra r - l term does not break the container argument because the width only shrinks as pointers move inward, exactly as in the classic problem.
